## Goal

Explain what an ion-selective cell measures, invert a logarithmic calibration,
and use independent checks without confusing a passing reference with proof
of sample-matrix compatibility. Keep activity and free-ion concentration distinct
from total element amount.

## Background

A potentiometric cell measures an indicator/reference potential difference
with negligible measurement current. Under a stated convention,
$E=K+(2.303RT/zF)\log_{10}a_i$, where $a_i=\gamma_i c_i/c^\circ$ is dimensionless
activity and $z$ is signed charge. The ideal 25 °C monovalent magnitude is about
59.16 mV per decade; this fluoride convention has a negative slope.

A calibration using concentration assumes an appropriate activity relationship
between samples and standards. Its model is
$E=a+b\log_{10}[c/(1\,\mathrm{mol/L})]$, hence
$c=10^{(E-a)/b}$ mol/L. Matched ionic strength can help but does not remove every
interference. These data and all model truths are simulated.

## By hand

**B1.** A model has $a=-97.42$ mV and $b=-59.16$ mV/decade. Calculate potential
at $1.00\times10^{-4}$ mol/L and concentration at 121.20 mV. Explain both inverse
steps. [Hint](#hint-b1)

**B2.** Decrease a fluoride reading by 17.8 mV. Predict whether inferred
concentration rises or falls and calculate its approximate factor.
[Hint](#hint-b2)

**B3.** Standards and a sample have identical free-ion concentration, but the
sample's activity coefficient is half the calibration coefficient. With no
drift, what concentration ratio will the old calibration infer? Could a
separate matrix-matched check still pass? [Hint](#hint-b3)

**B4.** An independent $10^{-4}$ mol/L check is expected at 138.98 mV. Readings
are 139.10 early and 145.00 later. Apply the supplied ±2.00 mV error rule. Is a
passing check evidence of exactly zero bias? [Hint](#hint-b4)

## Explore {#explore}

The model separates a sample-specific activity mismatch from a shared potential
drift. Its known input is visible only because it is a simulation. It withholds
a known mismatched sample even when reference and range checks pass.

**E1.** Keep drift zero. Change the sample/standard activity ratio to 0.50 and
compare true input, candidate estimate and check status. Explain the two
concentration positions at the same voltage. [Hint](#hint-e1)

**E2.** Restore matched conditions, set drift to +1 mV, then +6 mV. Compare
acceptance with actual concentration bias. What should happen before reporting
a result from the failed condition? [Hint](#hint-e2)

**E3.** Use the ideal matching switch after changing the ratio. Explain what
this switch assumes and name one chemical or instrumental error it does not
simulate. Export one scenario for inspection in R. [Hint](#hint-e3)

## In R

Run this complete workflow from the project root. The `log10()` transformation
is new only in chemical context; `lm()` and ID-based joins are familiar.

```r
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
standards <- read_csv("data/course/electrode-standards.csv",
                      show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(log_c = log10(fluoride_mol_l))
fit <- lm(potential_mv ~ log_c, data = standards)
a <- unname(coef(fit)[1]); b <- unname(coef(fit)[2])
ggplot(standards, aes(log_c, potential_mv)) + geom_point() +
  geom_abline(intercept = a, slope = b) +
  labs(x = "log10[c/(1 mol/L)]", y = "Potential (mV)") + theme_minimal()
checks <- read_csv("data/course/electrode-checks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(expected_mv = a + b * log10(check_fluoride_mol_l),
         error_mv = potential_mv - expected_mv,
         check_pass = abs(error_mv) <= allowed_abs_error_mv)
unknowns <- data.frame(block = c("early", "late"), potential_mv = c(121.2, 127.2)) |>
  left_join(select(checks, block, check_pass), by = "block") |>
  mutate(candidate_mol_l = 10^((potential_mv - a) / b),
         in_range = candidate_mol_l >= min(standards$fluoride_mol_l) &
                    candidate_mol_l <= max(standards$fluoride_mol_l),
         reported_mol_l = if_else(check_pass & in_range, candidate_mol_l, NA_real_))
coef(fit)
checks
unknowns
write_csv(unknowns, "output/potentiometry-exercise.csv", na = "NA")
```

**R1.** Interpret slope and intercept with their units and convention. Why does
`log10(0)` not supply a usable ordinary standard? [Hint](#hint-r1)

**R2.** Report the supported early value and the reason the late value is
withheld. Distinguish an algebraic candidate from a reported concentration.
[Hint](#hint-r2)

**R3.** Use the fitted slope to calculate the concentration factor from a
17.8 mV decrease. Explain why symmetric voltage limits become asymmetric
concentration limits. [Hint](#hint-r3)

## Hints

::: {#hint-b1 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="B1: undo the logarithm"}
At $10^{-4}$ mol/L, the explanatory value is −4. After solving for the log
concentration, raise 10 to that power.
:::
::: {#hint-b2 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="B2: respect the negative slope"}
The ratio is $10^{\Delta E/b}$, not $\Delta E/b$ itself.
:::
::: {#hint-b3 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="B3: activity ratio"}
The sample has half the activity at the same concentration. The check need not
share the sample-specific activity coefficient.
:::
::: {#hint-b4 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="B4: compare absolute errors"}
Subtract expected potential, then compare absolute errors with 2.00 mV. A
nonzero error can lie inside the acceptance interval.
:::
::: {#hint-e1 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="E1: the check has a different matrix"}
The reference is under calibration conditions. The sample-specific ratio does
not change its response in this model.
:::
::: {#hint-e2 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="E2: acceptance is not exactness"}
Both drifts change concentration. Only one exceeds the selected check tolerance.
:::
::: {#hint-e3 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="E3: an ideal control is an assumption"}
The switch sets the ratio exactly to one. Real adjustment does not prove the
absence of interfering ions, complexes or junction changes.
:::
::: {#hint-r1 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="R1: finite explanatory values"}
[`log10`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/Log.html) is undefined as a finite value at zero;
changing the concentration unit changes the intercept convention.
:::
::: {#hint-r2 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="R2: preserve evidence with IDs"}
Inspect both the check table and the joined unknown table. `NA` here is a
withheld estimate, not zero fluoride.
:::
::: {#hint-r3 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="R3: exponentiate both limits"}
The inverse is exponential. Equal positive/negative voltage deviations map to
reciprocal concentration factors rather than equal additive concentration changes.
:::

## Solutions

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Full worked solutions"}
**B1.** $E=-97.42+(-59.16)(-4)=139.22$ mV. For 121.20 mV,
$\log_{10}[c/(1\,\mathrm{mol/L})]=(121.20+97.42)/(-59.16)\approx-3.6954$;
$c\approx2.016\times10^{-4}$ mol/L. The log value itself is not concentration.
These hand coefficients are the ideal demo model, not the fitted dataset below.

**B2.** Factor $10^{-17.8/(-59.16)}\approx1.999$. A lower fluoride potential
means higher inferred concentration in this signed convention.

**B3.** The candidate is half the true free-ion concentration. A check under
calibration matrix conditions still has ratio one and can pass. It therefore
cannot establish this sample's calibration transfer. The known mismatch should
prevent a justified sample result until corrected or evaluated appropriately.

**B4.** Errors are +0.12 and +6.02 mV. The early check passes and later check
fails. The early error is nevertheless nonzero: the rule permits a bounded
error, not perfect accuracy.

**E1.** At ratio 0.50 and drift zero, candidate concentration is half the input,
while the check passes. The true-input point lies on the shifted sample line;
the inverse point lies on the old calibration at the same potential. Only the
simulation exposes the true concentration.

**E2.** +1 mV passes but gives concentration factor $10^{1/(-59.16)}\approx0.962$;
+6 mV fails and gives factor about 0.792. Investigate the failure, establish
satisfactory calibration/checks and remeasure affected samples. Do not assume
the failed check identifies its cause or supplies a universal correction.

**E3.** Ideal matching sets the sample/standard activity-coefficient ratio to
one. It does not model or eliminate interfering-ion effects, speciation,
reference-junction changes, temperature effects or recovery. These remain
chemical assumptions to evaluate rather than automatic consequences of a switch.

**R1.** Fitted intercept is **−97.42 mV**, slope **−59.10 mV per decade** for
concentration in mol/L relative to 1 mol/L. Zero has no finite log value.
Calibrating in another unit without altering the intercept gives the wrong
inverse convention.

**R2.** The accepted early estimate is **1.99915 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L**. The later
+6.02 mV check error fails; its reported concentration is `NA` even though code
can compute a candidate. The fixed matrix assumptions remain necessary for the
early result; passing the check does not prove them for arbitrary samples.

**R3.** The fitted-data factor is $10^{-17.8/(-59.10)}\approx2.001$:

```r
factor_from_decrease <- 10^(-17.8 / b)
factor_from_decrease
```

For a voltage uncertainty bound $\pm u_E$, multiplicative concentration factors
are $10^{\pm u_E/b}$. Their differences from one are unequal, producing
asymmetric concentration limits. A voltage SD must not be relabelled as a
concentration SD.
:::
